result.setting: Bone and Joint Center ward (88 beds) of a tertiary Class III Grade A general hospital, Henan Provincial People's Hospital, Zhengzhou
result.standard: 10 JBI-style review indicators derived from best evidence on perioperative oral nutritional supplements (ONS) in elderly hip fracture, e.g. staff ONS training (pass ≥80 points), NRS2002 screening within 24 h of admission, 24 h after surgery and before discharge, energy 25–30 kcal/(kg·d) and protein 1.0–1.5 g/kg, ONS 400–600 mL/d after surgery, post-discharge ONS 400 kcal and 30 g protein daily

cycle1.result: Compliance 0–10.7% across the 10 review indicators: staff training 10.7% (3/28); patient/caregiver education, screening, energy/protein targets, ONS use, disease-specific ONS, stopping rule, GI monitoring and discharge follow-up all 0%. Staff knowledge score 61.07±12.36.

result.intervention: Nurse-led multidisciplinary team with nutrition support nurses; daily 20-minute staff training over five days; updated NRS2002 form in the nursing IT system with fixed screening time points and automated reminders; 24-hour dietary energy and protein record sheet; dietary lists, leaflets, education manuals, QR codes, videos and teach-back; ward ONS supply protocol; discharge follow-up manual and smart cloud follow-up platform.

cycle2.result: Compliance 25–100% (all P < 0.05): 100% for indicators 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9; staff training 82.1% (23/28); ONS twice daily after surgery 56.8% (25/44); post-discharge ONS 25.0% (11/44). Staff knowledge score 85.57±16.89 (t = 6.195, P < 0.001).

result.other_findings: Discharge NRS2002 fell from 3.80±0.41 to 2.77±0.42 (P < 0.001) and patients at nutritional risk at discharge fell from 49/49 to 34/44 (P = 0.001); discharge albumin, length of stay and complications did not change significantly. Post-discharge nutritional follow-up stayed poor at 25%.

result.topic: COVID-19 infection and mortality in hip fracture
result.setting: Multicentre collaboration (IMPACT Global Hip Fracture Audit) of 112 hospitals in 14 countries
result.country: Multinational (Australia, Argentina, Chile, Cyprus, England, India, Italy, Greece, Mexico, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Spain, Sudan, Wales)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 651 (9.2%) patients had COVID-19: 225 (34.6%) positive at presentation and 426 (65.4%) positive postoperatively. 30-day survival 72.7% with COVID-19 versus 92.6% without (p < 0.001); COVID-19 independently associated with 30-day mortality (HR 2.83, p < 0.001).

result.other_findings: Positive COVID-19 status was associated with male sex, residential care, inpatient fall, ASA grade 4–5 and longer admission; length of stay of 10 days or more predicted postoperative COVID-19 (AUC 71.6%). Among COVID-19-positive patients, older age, male sex, renal disease and pulmonary disease predicted 30-day mortality.

result.topic: Pelvic fracture deaths in autopsy-based trauma audit
result.setting: Athens Forensic Medical Department, medico-legal autopsies of fatal falls (Attica Trauma Audit and Research Autopsy-Based Registry)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 209 (21.5%) of 970 fatal falls had pelvic fracture. Median ISS 50 (17-75) versus 26 (1-75) in controls (p < 0.0001); 163 (78%) potentially preventable deaths (ISS < 75); only 6 (2.9%) deaths directly attributed to pelvic fracture; pre-hospital mortality 70.3% versus 42.7% (p < 0.001).

result.other_findings: 126 (60.3%) of the pelvic fracture group had another injury code denoting major haemorrhage; median post-traumatic survival was 30 minutes versus 20 hours in controls. Psychiatric history had about 300% higher odds in the pelvic fracture group (OR 4.18).

result.topic: Open fracture antibiotic and tetanus prophylaxis
result.setting: Hospital João XXIII (Fundação Hospitalar de Minas Gerais), state public hospital specialised in urgency and trauma, Belo Horizonte
result.standard: Institutional Clinical Protocol 'Primary Treatment of Exposed Fractures' (FHEMIG, 2014): preoperative antibiotics; regimen by Gustilo type (cefazolin 1 g IV 6-hourly ± gentamicin 240 mg daily ± metronidazole 500 mg 6-hourly); duration 24 hours for types I and II and 72 hours for type III; tetanus prophylaxis according to vaccination history

cycle1.result: Preoperative antibiotics prescribed in 221 (91.7%); 59.3% (99/167) received a regimen not recommended by the protocol; 58.0% (254/438) of antibiotic doses were inconsistent; 63.5% of courses had an inadequate duration (95.6% of type I and II given > 24 hours); only 34 (14.1%) patients immunised against tetanus and vaccination history missing in 207 (85.9%).

result.other_findings: Gustilo classification was not recorded in 39.4% of patients; infection occurred in 18.7% and was associated with type III fractures, postoperative antibiotic start and antibiotics started more than 3 hours after admission. Mean time to surgery was 4 hours 12 minutes, with 82.6% operated within 6 hours.

result.setting: The Aga Khan University Hospital, tertiary care academic level-1 trauma hospital, orthopaedic trauma registry
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 177 patients with 189 fractures (113 lower limb, 76 upper limb); 176 (93.1%) had surgery. Radiological outcomes at about 3 months, e.g. radial shaft union excellent in 10/10 (100%), ulnar union excellent in 10/12 (83.3%), distal radius excellent in 3, good in 4 and poor in 1 of 8 assessed.

result.other_findings: Follow-up radiological data were available for only a subset of fractures (e.g. 5 of 13 humeral shaft, 4 of 13 femoral shaft, 14 of 26 tibial shaft). 34 of 47 (72.3%) proximal femur fractures had no in-hospital systemic complication.

result.setting: Fragility Fracture Network multiphase co-creation QI initiative; pilot-tested in five hospitals across four countries
result.standard: Evidence-based nutrition care recommendations for hip fracture (SIMPLER Six), e.g. interventions within 72 h (target 24 h) of presentation

cycle1.result: Two bi-national audits (n = 965, 63 hospitals), a global clinician survey (n = 308, 46 countries) and 15 interviews confirmed nutrition guidelines were routinely unmet; no numerical compliance figures given

result.intervention: Co-created SIMPLER Nutrition Pathway, protocol and toolkit, adapted locally through PDSA action–reflection cycles at pilot sites
result.other_findings: Paper describes pathway development and proposes core audit measures; effectiveness outcomes are to be reported separately. 46 services in 23 countries have committed to implementing SIMPLER.

result.setting: Specialist dental implant practice (private practice)
result.standard: Published abutment fracture rate from literature review: median 2.2% (all studies) and 1.8% (Ankylos-specific studies)

cycle1.result: Overall abutment fracture rate 0.6% (105/17,207), 1.6% below the 2.2% literature rate and 1.2% below the 1.8% Ankylos rate; first molar fracture rate 1.9% (87/4,709)

result.other_findings: Fractures were more common in men (2.6% vs 1.3% of first molars, p = 0.0015), with 89% opposing a natural tooth, 77% with gonial angle <120° and mean 74.3 months in function; 96% of implants were saved. Risk factors are to be shared with clinicians for consent and planning.

result.setting: 101 NHS hospital trauma and orthopaedic departments, national trainee-led multicentre audit (BOTA)
result.standard: JCST Core Quality Indicators 10 (minimum 5 consultant-supervised sessions per week) and 16 (2 trauma and 1 elective operating sessions and at least 1 fracture clinic per week)

cycle1.result: QI 10 met by 51/200 (25.5%) CSTs; QI 16 met by 11/200 (5.5%); both standards met by 10/200 (5%)

result.other_findings: Across all 935 junior doctors, time was spent 8.5% in theatre, 3.2% in clinic, 34.6% on ward cover and 20.7% on zero sessions. CSTs spent 31% on training activities versus 12% for non-CST doctors (p < 0.0001).

result.topic: COVID-19 infection and mortality after foot and ankle surgery
result.setting: 43 NHS centres, national multicentre retrospective audit (BOFAS)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: COVID-19 in 0.52% (n = 35); all-cause 30-day mortality 0.41%, 25.71% (n = 9) in COVID-19-positive patients; OR for mortality with COVID-19 11.71 (95% CI 1.55 to 88.74; p = 0.017)

result.other_findings: Surgical complications 6.07% and non-surgical 2.05%, unchanged across pre-lockdown, lockdown and post-lockdown periods. Post-lockdown COVID-19 rate was 0.15% with no COVID-19 deaths; diabetic foot surgery carried the highest risk.

result.topic: Hip fracture national registry quality indicators
result.setting: Dutch Hip Fracture Audit, nationwide registry (66/68 hospitals in 2020)
result.standard: DHFA quality indicators: surgery within 48 h, osteoporosis assessment, orthogeriatric co-management (age 70+), registration of functional outcomes at 3 months, case-mix adjusted 30-day mortality

cycle1.result: Mean observed hospital percentages 2016 vs 2020: surgery <48 h 91.1% vs 93.0%; osteoporosis assessment 48.0% vs 35.8%; orthogeriatric co-management 70.1% vs 77.6%; functional outcome registration 28.8% vs 43.2%. Mixed-model 2017–2020: time to surgery p = 0.16, osteoporosis p = 0.68, orthogeriatric p = 0.51, functional outcomes p < 0.01, 30-day mortality p = 0.21

result.other_findings: Missing clinical values fell from 7.5% (2016) to 3.2% (2020) and 3-month follow-up completeness rose from 36.2% to 46.8%. Osteoporosis assessment stayed poor with wide between-hospital variation (best hospital 86.1%).

result.setting: Warrington Hospital, district general hospital; inpatients aged 65 and over with fragility fractures
result.standard: Six Standards of Hip Care (assessment for antiresorptive medication after fragility fracture) and NOGG UK 2021 guidance; NICE recommendations on vitamin D and bone protection

cycle1.result: Inpatient bisphosphonates started in 23/144 (16%); 105/121 (87%) not started by GP after discharge; FRAX recorded in 78/144 (54%); vitamin D assessed in 89/144 (62%) and replaced in 78/144 (54%); 110/144 no DEXA scan; 34/144 (25%) referred to metabolic bone clinic

result.intervention: Teaching sessions, MDT meetings and bedside teaching; local protocol flowcharts; push to start antiresorptives before discharge; new orthogeriatrics SHO role; new older people osteoporosis clinic

cycle2.result: 105/165 (64%) did not receive appropriate bisphosphonates (34 started as inpatients); 104/131 (around 80%) not started by GP after discharge; FRAX recorded in 30/165 (18%); vitamin D checked in 57/165 (35%) and 99/165 (60%) received no replacement; DEXA and bone clinic referrals remained low

result.other_findings: Only minor improvement in inpatient bisphosphonate prescribing; the osteoporosis clinic opened about six months late. Patients discharged from the emergency department were often not assessed, so an SOP and electronic alerts were proposed.

result.setting: Department of Orthopaedics, The Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University (tertiary hospital), Hebei Province; primary unilateral TKA patients
result.standard: not reported (institutional DVT prevention protocol with Caprini assessment; failure modes with RPN > 125 treated as high risk)

cycle1.result: DVT incidence 16/68 (23.53%); length of stay 11.20 ± 4.21 days; 6-week HSS score 76.80 ± 6.90; RPN for the eight high-risk failure modes ranged from 129.79 to 247.88.

result.intervention: Integrated FMEA-RCA programme: multidisciplinary team, workflow mapping, dual nurse-physician Caprini verification, electronic reminders, ISBAR handover checklist, PBL/CBL staff training, HAPA-based patient education with WeChat videos, and head-nurse supervision with twice-weekly spot-check audits.

cycle2.result: DVT incidence 4/68 (5.88%) vs 23.53% (χ2 = 8.442, P = 0.004; aOR 0.24, 95% CI 0.08–0.72, P = 0.011); length of stay 7.99 ± 2.06 days (P < 0.001); 6-week HSS 82.30 ± 5.60 (P < 0.001); all eight RPN values lower (mean relative reduction 36.29%).

result.other_findings: Quasi-experimental before-after comparison of outcomes rather than an audit against a standard; process compliance indicators were monitored but their results are not reported in the text. Largest RPN fall was for poor implementation of postoperative prevention measures (247.88 to 99.73).

result.setting: Orthogeriatric Unit, Northwick Park Hospital, Harrow/London; patients aged 65 and over with acute hip fracture needing surgery
result.standard: BOAST hip fracture standards and NICE guidance on cognitive assessment; AMTS documented at admission, postoperative days 1 and 2, and day 4; target 80% compliance

cycle1.dates: Dates stated inconsistently: July–November 2023 (abstract) or 1 January to 31 March 2024 (methods)
cycle1.result: Initial AMTS 14/30 (46.7%); postoperative day 1 0/30 (0%); postoperative day 2 0/30 (0%); day 4 19/30 (63.3%); overall 33/120 assessments (27.5%).

result.intervention: Automated Cerner EPR alerts prompting AMTS at set timepoints, mandatory 90-minute staff training, AMTS built into handover and ward round templates, visual reminders, and monthly audit feedback.

cycle2.dates: Dates stated inconsistently: November 2023 to January 2024 (abstract) or 1 July to 30 September 2024 (methods)

result.other_findings: Day 4 orthogeriatric AMTS fell and declined month by month in cycle 2 (68% to 41%), suggesting intervention fatigue; no timepoint reached the 80% target. Appropriate responses to abnormal scores rose from 67% to 89%.

result.topic: COVID-19 impact on foot and ankle surgical activity
result.setting: 43 centres across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; adults having foot and ankle surgery in theatre (national multicentre retrospective audit)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: COVID-19 in 35/6644 (0.53%) overall: 0.40% pre-lockdown, 2.11% during lockdown, 0.16% post-lockdown; activity during lockdown 24.44% of pre-lockdown, elective activity 1.73% during and 10.72% after lockdown.

result.other_findings: Infection rates varied by region (highest South East 1.12%, cumulative peak 3.21%); regional anaesthesia use rose significantly during and after lockdown and day-case rates fell.

result.setting: Secondary analysis of the national Physiotherapy Hip Fracture Sprint Audit (England and Wales), linked to HES and PEDW; patients aged 60 and over with surgery for first non-pathological hip fracture
result.standard: Chartered Society of Physiotherapy hip fracture standards cited: minimum total of two hours of physiotherapy in the first postoperative week, physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation within a day of surgery (not used as an audit target in the analysis)

cycle1.dates: Patients operated on in May or June 2017
cycle1.result: ≥2 h physiotherapy in first week: 228 (42.1%) with depression vs 1992 (44.6%) without; physiotherapy on 6–7 days: 91 (16.8%) vs 875 (19.6%). Adjusted OR per 30-min increase for readmission 0.89 (0.81–0.98) vs 0.97 (0.93–1.00), interaction p = 0.09.

result.other_findings: Observational analysis of associations between physiotherapy dose and outcomes by depression diagnosis; no formal interaction reached significance.

result.specialty: Health services research (multiple surgical specialties including orthopaedic trauma)
result.topic: Acceptance of claims-based audit and feedback
result.setting: Online focus groups with medical specialists from 17 academic, top-clinical and general hospitals
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Qualitative study: specialists had mixed views; concerns were validity and reliability of claims data, lack of clinical interpretation and misuse by insurers. Acceptance was higher when feedback comes via professional associations and is not used to judge performance.

result.topic: Fracture liaison service key performance indicators
result.setting: International position paper (IOF Capture the Fracture Working Group, National Osteoporosis Foundation and Fragility Fracture Network)
result.standard: Eleven patient-level FLS KPIs adapted from the UK FLS Database audit; achievement levels red <50%, amber 50–79%, green ≥80% (treatment recommendation target 50%)

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Useful source of audit standards for FLS: e.g. assessment and DXA within 12 weeks, falls assessment, AOM started and follow-up within 16 weeks, AOM persistence at 52 weeks, and data completeness.

result.setting: District general hospital trauma and orthopaedic department (population 320,000, consultant-led 24/7 trauma service)
result.standard: GMC and Royal College of Physicians documentation recommendations: clearly documented PTWR, date/time, consultant on take, clinician leading and documenting, presenting complaint and management plan

cycle1.result: 72% seen on PTWR, 47% of these clearly labelled; 64% of those not seen were weekend admissions; no consultant on take identifiable in 19%, presenting complaint missing in 78%, no plan in 3%, not timed in 17%, no name 19%, no signature 14%, no grade 50%, no contact details 25%.

result.intervention: Trauma Meeting/Post-Take Ward Round proforma on yellow paper, designed with the team (PDSA cycles), results presented at departmental teaching, and weekend surgical juniors briefed to attend the trauma meeting and complete it.

cycle2.dates: Prospective re-audit two weeks after implementation
cycle2.result: Not seen on PTWR fell from 28% to 18% (4% weekend admissions); 88% of those seen had a proforma; 18% of all cases had no proforma; consultant unidentifiable in 4%; all entries signed and dated; no name 12%, no contact details 15%, no grade 10%.

result.other_findings: Weekend proforma completion stayed poor (67% of cases without a proforma were weekend admissions); all remaining documentation gaps were in cases without a proforma.

result.setting: Carle Hospital, Urbana, Illinois; hospitalised hip fracture patients (prospective QI project with medical record audit)
result.standard: Evidence-based delirium prevention protocol; records audited with the CHART-DEL instrument

cycle1.result: Delirium incidence 11.1% (pre-implementation).

result.intervention: Evidence-based hip fracture delirium prevention protocol introduced.

cycle2.result: Delirium incidence 15.6% (not statistically significant); protocol used by admitting physicians in 31% of admissions; prevention interventions documented by nurses in 75.6% of records.

result.other_findings: Abstract only; low physician uptake of the protocol (31%).

result.topic: VTE prophylaxis after hip and knee arthroplasty
result.setting: 31 hospitals performing more than 250 hip and/or knee arthroplasties a year; cluster-randomised crossover trial nested in the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Statistical analysis plan for the CRISTAL trial (aspirin 85–150 mg vs enoxaparin 40 mg); recruitment stopped early after an interim analysis met the stopping rule. Protocol compliance was audited on the first 20 patients per arm, with re-education and re-audit until compliance exceeded 80%.

result.topic: Open fracture management against BOAST standards
result.setting: National Trauma Audit and Research Network (TARN) data from up to 190 NHS hospitals; registry-based incidence and quality-of-care study
result.standard: BOAST 4 / Open Fracture BOAST and National Major Trauma Centre Dashboard standards (e.g. debridement within 12 hours, soft-tissue coverage within 72 hours, combined orthoplastic plan, antibiotics within one hour)

cycle1.result: Of 12,170 severe open tibial fractures: median time to debridement 13.0 hours (IQR 6.4 to 20.9); debridement within 12 hours 24% overall (22% 2008–2011, 28% 2012–2015, 21% 2016–2019); soft-tissue coverage within 72 hours 4% (2008–2011) rising to 35% (2016–2019); first debridement with consultant orthopaedic and plastic surgeons present 10% (n = 1,175).

result.other_findings: Missing data exceeded 25% overall and reached 83–85% for some standards, limiting interpretation. Six of 13 BOAST standards declined between 2012–2015 and 2016–2019; overall open fracture incidence 2012–2019 was 6.94 per 100,000 person-years.

result.topic: Hip fracture national audit quality indicators
result.setting: Dutch Hip Fracture Audit (DHFA), nationwide registry; 60 of 81 Dutch hospitals participating
result.standard: Dutch guidelines 'Proximal Femur Fracture' (2016) and 'Multidisciplinary Treatment of Frail Elderly During Surgical Procedures' (2016); national guideline states every patient over 70 should receive orthogeriatric management

cycle1.result: Case ascertainment 58% (10,612 of 18,385 operated patients); variable completeness 77% (91% at discharge, 30% at 3 months); median time to surgery 18 h (IQR 7–23) for ASA 1–2 and 21 h (IQR 13–27) for ASA 3–4; 78% of operated patients aged 70 and over received orthogeriatric management.

result.other_findings: Describes set-up of the national audit; significant variation between hospitals on all three indicators (e.g. 29–75% of ASA 1–2 patients operated within 18 h). Only 23% of older patients were treated on a dedicated orthogeriatric ward.

result.topic: Open fracture time to debridement and soft-tissue cover
result.setting: Trauma Audit and Research Network (TARN) data from 175 hospitals (major trauma centres and other hospitals); registry cohort study
result.standard: Open Fracture BOAST: debridement within 12 hours and soft-tissue coverage within 72 hours

cycle1.result: Debridement within 12 hours in 2,052 patients (46%), median time 13.6 hours (IQR 6.4 to 20.9); soft-tissue coverage within 72 hours in 2,187 (63%), median 47.8 hours (IQR 15.9 to 111.5). Evening presentation (16:00 to 23:59) less likely to meet debridement standard (RR 0.56); Thursday/Friday presentation (RR 0.88/0.89) and non-MTC care (RR 0.76) less likely to meet coverage standard.

result.other_findings: Time to debridement was missing for 45% and time to soft-tissue coverage for 52% of patients, mostly from non-MTC hospitals. Proportion meeting the 72-hour coverage target rose from 44% to 69% between 2012 and 2015.

result.setting: Secondary analysis of UK Physiotherapy Hip Fracture Sprint Audit linked to National Hip Fracture Database, HES, PEDW and ONS data; hospitals in England and Wales
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 20% (1,026) received physiotherapy on 6–7 of 7 days in the first postoperative week. Adjusted odds ratio of discharge 1.26 (95% CI 1.19–1.33) per additional day of physiotherapy and 1.33 (95% CI 1.12–1.57) for ≥ 2 h vs < 2 h; physiotherapy type not associated with discharge.

result.other_findings: Authors propose a 7-day physiotherapy service totalling at least 2 h in the first postoperative week as a key performance indicator; estimated saving of 456 bed-days a year for an average hospital.

result.setting: Scottish Hip Fracture Audit national registry linked to national hospital and mortality records; retrospective cohort
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: CFS completed in 8,573 of 15,546 patients (55%). Mortality aHR 1.77 (95% CI 1.52 to 2.06) for CFS 4–5, 3.01 (2.59 to 3.50) for CFS 6–8 and 9.95 (7.03 to 14.09) for CFS 9 vs CFS 1–3; one-year mortality AUC 0.72 for CFS vs 0.66 for ASA.

result.other_findings: CFS was a non-mandated registry variable, explaining low completion. CFS predicted return to original residence within 30 days only moderately (AUC 0.63 vs 0.61 for ASA).

result.setting: Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust; trauma and elective orthopaedic surgery across both sites
result.standard: BOAST 'The Safe Use of Intraoperative Tourniquets': document exsanguination method, isolation method, skin condition, pressure and duration; pressure lower limb SBP + 70–130 mmHg, upper limb SBP + 50–100 mmHg; duration ideally < 120 min

cycle1.result: Exsanguination method documented 5.6%, isolation (shut-off drape) 2.4%, skin condition 0%; duration not in operative note 23.0%, not recorded at all 1.6%; > 120 min in 1.6%; pressure within standard in 24.3% lower limb, 34.8% upper limb and 66.7% paediatric cases.

result.intervention: Local presentation at trust Quality & Safety Half Day and 'PRESSURE' mnemonic posters in theatres and offices, followed by a new electronic patient record with a tourniquet section and BOAST-based auto-text proforma in the operation note.

cycle2.result: Exsanguination method documented 42.9% (p = 0.001), isolation 42.9% (p = 0.0001), skin condition 64.3% (p = 0.0001); duration not in operative note 10.2% (p = 0.0269), not recorded 0%; none > 120 min; pressure within standard 13.0% lower limb, 35.7% upper limb, 14.2% paediatric (no significant change).

result.other_findings: An interim re-audit in March 2022 after education alone (n = 153) showed little change (e.g. exsanguination 9.8%, skin condition 5.2%). Staff survey (n = 19) found over 50% sized tourniquets on 'whatever looks the best fit' and 31.6% did not know paediatric pressures.

result.setting: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, single academic tertiary centre (four hospital sites); automated EHR-based audit
result.standard: NICE Quality Standard QS138 statement 2 (pre-2026 definition): adults having surgery with expected blood loss >500 mL should receive perioperative tranexamic acid

cycle1.result: Overall automated TXA compliance 78.7%.

cycle2.result: Overall automated TXA compliance 86.3% (manual QI audit same period 90%, 10 cases); trauma and orthopaedics 98.2% (n = 393), cardiac surgery 83.7%, gynaecology 83.2%, urology 94.2%, colorectal 43.5%, vascular 0%. Improvement from 2024 included gynaecology +26.8% and cardiac surgery +15.6%.

result.other_findings: Paper is mainly a validation of an automated audit: denominator coverage 96.2%, miscoding 3.9%, WHO checklist–EPR concordance 74.2%, and manually adjudicated 'true' compliance 85.3%. Primary hip and knee replacements 98.8%, revision hip and knee 100%, neck of femur fracture fixation 96.7%; open iliofemoral and aortic operations 0%.

result.topic: National hip fracture audit standards compliance
result.setting: Irish Hip Fracture Database national clinical audit, all 16 eligible acute hospitals in Ireland (NOCA, RCSI)
result.standard: Irish Hip Fracture Standards (seven core clinical standards, 2017; based on BOA/BGS Blue Book standards) and best practice tariff criteria; data quality target of 90% case submission

cycle1.result: Geriatrician assessment 11%, bone health assessment 65%, falls assessment 62%, surgery within 48 h 70%, admission from ED to orthopaedic ward 15%; national coverage 63%.

result.intervention: Establishment of the national audit with governance committee, audit manager, hospital hip fracture governance committees, quarterly dashboards with SPC charts, a QI foundation programme, a best practice tariff (€1000 per compliant case, from 2018), the Golden Hip Award, and new orthogeriatric and advanced nurse practitioner posts.

cycle2.result: Geriatrician assessment 86%, bone health assessment 90%, falls assessment 87%, surgery within 48 h 77%, admission from ED to orthopaedic ward 36%; national coverage 95%; day one physiotherapy mobilisation 74% (2018) to 85%.

result.other_findings: Total 41,304 cases 2013–2024; best practice tariff compliance rose from 7% (2018) to 21% (2024) and time to surgery remained the hardest standard to meet. Inpatient mortality fell from 5% to 4% and new long-term care admission from 6% to 3%.

result.setting: Orthogeriatric unit (experimental) versus conventional orthopaedic unit (control), Grenoble Alpes University Hospital; controlled before/after audit and feedback study
result.standard: Unit pain protocol: routine acetaminophen 1 g three times a day (3 g/day) during the three postoperative days

cycle1.dates: December 2018 to April 2019 (before intervention, started May 2019)
cycle1.result: Postoperative 3 g/day acetaminophen 16% (16/99); preoperative 9%; nurse adherence to acetaminophen prescriptions 13% preoperatively and 13% postoperatively.

result.intervention: Audit and feedback with nurses: two 1-hour pain teaching sessions, distribution of a pain assessment scale, protocol updated to 'give acetaminophen regardless of pain assessment', medicine staffing reviewed with clinical pharmacy, and night/weekend standby with a Saturday ward round.

cycle2.result: Postoperative 3 g/day acetaminophen 60% (60/100) (OR 8.55, p < 0.001; versus control OR 6.76, p < 0.001); preoperative 16% (p = 0.13); nurse adherence 32% preoperatively and 52% postoperatively.

result.other_findings: Control unit showed no change (postoperative 29.3% to 33.7%). Intervention failed preoperatively; ADL at discharge improved and unit stay fell by 2.5 days, with no change in complications.

result.setting: Changi General Hospital, 1000-bed hospital in eastern Singapore; anaesthesia department QI project
result.standard: Surgery within 48 hours of hip fracture; aims of a 10% increase in patients seen by anaesthesia within 24 hours and a 10% increase in surgery within 48 hours

cycle1.result: Median time to first anaesthesia consult 35.3 hours; consults <24 hours 39%; median time to surgery 61.5 hours; surgery within 48 hours 38%.

result.intervention: Consultant-led anaesthesia perioperative outreach service seeing patients within 24 hours of admission, with case manager notification, REDCap follow-up database, standardised workflow and guidelines, and 6-monthly PDSA audits.

cycle2.result: Median time to anaesthesia consult 21.5 hours (p = 0.029); consults <24 hours 67% (p < 0.003); median time to surgery 46 hours in results (50 hours in abstract) (p = 0.897); surgery within 48 hours 51.6% (p = 0.904).

result.other_findings: Median time to nerve block fell from 41 hours (2019) to 22 hours (2021); patients discharged within 10 days rose from 53.5% to 59.5%. Critical care reviews rose while ICU admissions fell.

result.setting: Sprint audit of 31 hospitals (24 Australia, 7 New Zealand) in the Australian and New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry; patients on DOACs versus other or no antithrombotics
result.standard: ANZ hip fracture clinical care standard and international consensus: surgery within 36 hours (including for patients on DOACs)

cycle1.result: Median time to surgery 39 h (IQR 24–48) on DOACs, 25 h (IQR 20–39) on no antithrombotic and 27 h (IQR 20–44) on other antithrombotics; DOAC patients had higher odds of surgery >36 h (aOR 3.65, 95% CI 2.40–5.55); 43% of DOAC patients had surgery within 36 h versus 61% on other antithrombotics.

result.other_findings: 18% (192) were on DOACs; transfusion rates did not differ (23% vs 17% vs 22%). Only 5/24 Australian and all 7 New Zealand hospitals had a DOAC protocol, and 73% restarted DOACs >48 h after surgery.

result.topic: Secondary fracture prevention after hip fracture
result.setting: Orthogeriatric co-managed ward, Beijing Jishuitan Hospital, tertiary hospital
result.standard: UK Fracture Liaison Service Database (FFFAP) key performance indicators (7 of 11 KPIs assessed), benchmarked against UK FFFAP 2016–2018 figures

cycle1.result: BMD screening 97.1% (2,610/2,689); bone-protective medication before discharge 94.0% (2,454/2,610); follow-up 50.7% at 90 days, 17.7% at 12–16 weeks, 9.5% at 12 months. 2018 KPIs: FLS assessment within 90 days 57.1% (UK 67.0%), falls assessment 87.5%, bone therapy recommended 94.3%, adherence at 12 months 11.6% (UK 18.8%).

result.other_findings: Falls assessment rose from 11.4% (2016) to 87.5% (2018) and DXA-only scanning fell to 14.1% in 2018 as QCT replaced it. Secondary fracture rates stayed at 11.0–13.4% across follow-up points.

result.topic: Proximal humeral fracture admission and length of stay
result.setting: Western Health, single large tertiary health service (Footscray, Sunshine and Williamstown hospitals); retrospective audit of records
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 39.4% (276) admitted to hospital; median length of stay 23 days (IQR 7, 48.5); 15.5% (109) needed a new discharge destination. Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index was associated with admission, longer stay and new discharge destination.

result.other_findings: Living with family/friends or in a care facility before injury was associated with lower admission and shorter stay; surgical treatment was associated with shorter stay (IRR 0.56). Older age and dementia were associated with a new discharge destination.

result.setting: IMPACT international multicentre audit collaboration (Scottish Hip Fracture Audit and partners); commentary
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Commentary on lessons from the IMPACT hip fracture audits in 2020, recommending reporting standards and a strategy for rapid collaborative audits and data-sharing in future outbreaks.

result.setting: not reported
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Title only: describes the rationale for criteria for a medical audit of total knee replacement.

result.topic: Supracondylar fracture management against appropriate use criteria
result.setting: Mansoura University Emergency Hospital, a tertiary referral centre in the Nile Delta
result.standard: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) appropriate use criteria (AUC) for paediatric supracondylar humerus fractures; primary outcome proportion of cases managed 'appropriately'

cycle1.result: 62.1% (36/58) managed 'appropriately'; 19.0% (11/58) 'rarely appropriate'; 19.0% (11/58) 'may be appropriate'. 65% of type IIa fractures were managed with casting alone ('rarely appropriate').

result.intervention: Cycle 2: mandatory 2-hour AUC workshop, pocket reference cards and a departmental protocol with a type II fracture flowchart. Cycle 3: three refresher workshops, AUC training in resident orientation, laminated AUC flowcharts in ED, theatre and ward, departmental grand round presentations, weekly case discussions and individualised audit feedback.

cycle2.result: 87.9% (51/58) managed 'appropriately' (25.8% absolute improvement from baseline); 'rarely appropriate' 3.4% (2/58); 'may be appropriate' 8.6% (5/58). AUC tool use documented in over 95% of cases.

result.other_findings: Intermediate cycle (September 2021–February 2022, n=62) showed 75.8% (47/62) appropriate and 9.7% (6/62) rarely appropriate, with AUC rating documented in only 45% of cases. At baseline 78% of surgeons were unfamiliar with the AUC web tool.

result.topic: Virtual fracture clinic referral and remote follow-up
result.setting: OLVG, a level 2 trauma centre and teaching hospital in Amsterdam (emergency department and virtual fracture clinic)
result.standard: Predefined standards from national coronavirus outpatient guidelines and local consensus: (1) all eligible ED trauma patients referred for VFC review; (2) all patients contacted after VFC review; (3) patient-initiated follow-up by default where possible; (4) follow-up by telephone or video where possible. Target 100% for standard 1.

cycle1.result: 162/184 (88.0%) referred for VFC review; 98.1% reached afterwards (3 patients, 1.9%, not reached); 29/162 (17.9%) discharged 'virtually'; 137/291 (45.0%) appointments remote. Median total ED time 95 minutes vs 131 minutes at baseline (p<0.001).

result.intervention: After an evaluation meeting, ED staff were invited to attend VFC review for direct feedback, presentations explaining the workflow were held, posters were put up in the ED, and a patient information leaflet asking patients to call if not contacted by 15:00 the next workday was introduced.

cycle2.result: 302/305 (98.4%) referred for VFC review; 99.0% reached afterwards (3 patients, 1.0%, not reached); 41/302 (13.6%) discharged 'virtually'; 179/436 (41.1%) appointments remote. Median total ED time 98 minutes (−33 minutes vs baseline, p=0.001); time to review 47 minutes (p<0.001); time for review 35 minutes vs 45 minutes (p=0.019).

result.other_findings: An ED orthopaedic trauma fast-track pathway was introduced alongside the VFC; 88% and 92% of suspected fracture patients were treated in fast-track rooms. Median VFC review time was 9 minutes then 7 minutes per patient.

result.setting: Nationwide Dutch Hip Fracture Audit registry covering 66 hospitals
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: Mortality 9.1% at 30 days, 15% at 90 days and 26% at 1 year. Logistic regression was preferred, with test-set c-statistics of 0.82 (30-day), 0.81 (90-day) and 0.80 (1-year).

result.other_findings: Registry-based machine learning prediction study, not an audit. ASA class, age and sex were the strongest predictors.

result.setting: Salford Royal NHS Foundation Trust, a major trauma centre in north-west England; rib fixation by orthopaedic surgeons with the multidisciplinary Chest Injuries Group
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: Mean 4.1 days from ED to rib fixation, critical care LOS 12.7 days, overall hospital LOS 29.1 days; mortality 3.3% (one death). In the matched cohort comparison, mortality was 36.7% conservative vs 3.3% rib fixation (p=0.001).

result.intervention: No specific intervention described; the re-audit reviewed the next cohort of rib fixation patients as the service developed.

cycle2.result: Mean 2.1 days from ED to rib fixation, critical care LOS 7.5 days and overall hospital LOS 20.7 days (LOS based on 17 patients); no deaths and no fixation-related complications.

result.other_findings: Matched cohort outcome study plus retrospective re-audit without a stated standard. No statistically significant differences in total hospital or ICU LOS between operative and conservative groups.

result.setting: Publicly funded community, sub-acute and acute podiatry services of Bendigo Health and Bendigo Community Health Services, regional Victoria
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: University of Texas risk: no neuropathy 296 (51.4%), neuropathy 144 (25.0%), history of pathology 75 (13.0%), active pathology 61 (10.6%). New ulceration in 36 (6.3%); history of pathology predicted ulceration (OR 8.1, 95% CI 3.6 to 18.2, p<0.001).

result.other_findings: Described as a prospective clinical audit but is a descriptive epidemiological study with no standard. Higher risk was associated with longer diabetes duration, male sex and type 1 diabetes.

result.setting: Vancouver General Hospital arthroplasty service ('Short Term Accelerated Recovery' STAR programme)
result.standard: Aim of >80% successful same-day discharge among eligible primary THA patients without compromising safety (unscheduled 30-day hospital encounters)

cycle1.result: Standard cohort: 57/105 (54.3%) discharged same day; complications preventing same-day discharge 48 (45.7%); unscheduled 30-day hospital encounters 11 (10.5%).

result.intervention: Enhanced Recovery Canada recommendations: pre-emptive nausea prophylaxis (aprepitant, scopolamine patch), pre-emptive multimodal oral analgesia, and lidocaine epidural anaesthesia via a 'STAR Module' in the electronic order set, supported by STAR rounds, website posts and a video; then a switch to spinal lidocaine.

cycle2.result: Spinal lidocaine cohort: 80.6% discharged same day vs 54.3% (OR 3.4, 95% CI 1.34 to 8.66, p=0.0102).

result.other_findings: Combined ERC cohort (February 2021–August 2024, n=129): 96 (74.4%) same-day discharge (OR 2.51, p=0.0015), complications preventing discharge 33 (25.6%), 30-day encounters 12 (9.3%), not significantly different. Transient neurological symptoms in 3/33 (9%) spinal lidocaine patients; lack of evening physiotherapy limited reassessment.

result.topic: Participation in national hip fracture audit
result.setting: Survey of Dutch orthopaedic and trauma surgeons about the Dutch Hip Fracture Audit
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.dates: Interviews 1 June 2017–8 November 2017; survey from November 2017
cycle1.result: Most agreed factors: staffing capacity for data collection (95.1%), automated data import (95.1%), financial support from hospital board (94.1%). Lower participation with academic hospital (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04–0.52) and orthopaedic surgeon (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.10–0.90); data sharing with external parties associated with active participation (OR 3.19, 95% CI 1.14–8.95).

result.other_findings: Survey of opinion rather than an audit; 51 (46.8%) respondents reported active participation (≥80% of patients registered).

result.setting: Foot and ankle orthopaedic telephone clinic, York Hospital, a district general hospital
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: Discharged 20 (19%); further face-to-face follow-up 52 (50%); further phone consult 12 (12%); did not attend 17 (17%); scans requested 5 (5%); listed for operation 2 (2%).

result.intervention: Orthopaedic clinician-led triage to select patients for telephone clinic.

cycle2.result: Discharged 44 (30%, p=0.030); further face-to-face follow-up 59 (40%, p=0.053); further phone consult 31 (21%, p=0.026); did not attend 13 (9%, p=0.033); scans requested 18 (12%, p=0.023); listed for operation 6 (4%, p=0.172).

result.other_findings: Described as a clinical audit but no explicit standard or target was stated. Among trauma patients alone, differences were not significant.

result.topic: Soft tissue knee injury pathway timescales and MRI use
result.setting: Acute knee clinic, Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (single NHS trust)
result.standard: NHS Constitution RTT standard (92% of consultant-led pathways completed within 18 weeks); Diagnostics DM01 standard (<1% waiting over six weeks for MRI); BOA/BOAST and regional MSK guidance of MRI within two weeks where diagnosis uncertain, with review within 7-14 days; NICE CKS and EBI guidance on selective MRI

cycle1.result: MRI utilisation 77.7% (269/346). Median waits: presentation to knee clinic 7 days, MRI referral to scan 33 days, scan to review 22 days; median presentation to diagnosis 60 days and to definitive management 97 days. 58.0% waited over four weeks for MRI; only 11.9% scanned within one week; 10.3% reviewed within seven days and 26.2% within 14 days. 42.8% of MRIs normal/degenerative.

result.other_findings: Surgery in 11.0% (38/346) with median 128 days from presentation to operation; only 7.2% of non-operative patients started physiotherapy within 30 days of clinic (median 70.5 days). GP referrals had longer median time to diagnosis (74 days) than UTC (53.5) or ED (58); a physiotherapy-first, criteria-based MRI pathway and re-audit were proposed.

result.topic: Fibreglass backslab offloading for plantar foot ulcers
result.setting: Multidisciplinary Diabetes Foot Unit and Podiatry clinics, Fiona Stanley Hospital, Perth (tertiary hospital)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 28 patients (29 ulcers); 19 patients (20 ulcers) continued the backslab device. At 12 weeks median ulcer area 0.25 (0-0.55) cm2 with median reduction 97 (80-100)%; 9 (45%) ulcers completely healed (median 71 days) and 11 (55%) achieved at least 50% reduction (median 24 days).

result.other_findings: Nine patients (31%) stopped the device (irritation, discomfort, non-compliance, change of offloading, lost to follow-up); no device complications were documented in those who used it.

result.topic: Long-term survival of cross-arch stabilising bridges in periodontitis
result.setting: Specialist periodontal private practice, Egersund (rural referral practice)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.dates: Bridges constructed 1986 to 2016; observed up to 35 years
cycle1.result: 111 bridges in 94 patients; 16 bridges (14.4%) failed after 16.1 years (SD 4.0). Abutment tooth loss 8.9% vs 34.4% from the rest of the same arch and 25.4% from the opposing arch (p < 0.0001). Failure associated with poor oral hygiene (p = 0.0093) and complications during maintenance (p = 0.0059).

result.other_findings: Bridges with distal cantilevers failed in 16% and tooth-implant combination bridges in 14.0%; patients reported good satisfaction. Abstract gives 98 patients but the text reports 94.

result.topic: COVID-19 green pathway infection and mortality in foot and ankle surgery
result.setting: 46 NHS centres performing foot and ankle surgery (UK-FAlCoN national audit)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.dates: Phase 1: 13 January 2020 to 31 July 2020; Phase 2: 1 September 2020 to 30 November 2020
cycle1.result: Perioperative COVID-19 infection 1.07% (69/6470) on blue pathways vs 0.21% (9/4271) on green pathways (P < .001). No significant difference in phase 1; in phase 2 green pathway infection 0.16% vs 2.14% (OR 0.077). 30-day mortality 0.54% blue vs 0.09% green (p < .001); no difference in COVID-19-related mortality.

result.other_findings: COVID-19-related mortality fell from 25.71% (9/35) in phase 1 to 4.65% (2/43) in phase 2 (p = .008). Elective patients on green pathways rose from 49.73% to 90.83% between phases.

result.setting: Princess Royal University Hospital, Orpington (district general hospital, King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust)
result.standard: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 42 (shoulder dystocia)

cycle1.result: Incidence 1.32% (56/4,247 vaginal deliveries). Emergency response activated in 98.2% (mean response 2.3 minutes); McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure first line in 80.4%; internal manoeuvres in 37.5%; mean head-to-body delivery after recognition 4.7 minutes. Maternal complications 53.6%, PPH 7.1%; neonatal complications 83.9%, resuscitation 26.8%, NICU 3.6%, no permanent brachial plexus injury.

result.other_findings: 30.4% of cases had no identifiable risk factor; third/fourth degree tears in 7.1% and transient brachial plexus palsy in 3.6%. Better documentation systems and longer follow-up were recommended.

result.topic: Non-surgical biomechanical device for knee osteoarthritis
result.setting: Circle Integrated Care MSK service, Bedfordshire (NHS community musculoskeletal pathway)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 65 (11.4%) referred for secondary care consultation over mean follow-up 3.5 years (mean 480.9 days to referral). WOMAC pain fell 43.2% (56.4 to 32.0 at 3 years), function improved 41.2%, OKS rose from 21.9 to 28.3 at 12 months and gait velocity rose 24.8% (all p < 0.05).

result.other_findings: 48% of referrals occurred in year 1 and 32% in year 2; there was no control group and actual knee replacement rates were not confirmed.

result.topic: Whole-body CT yield and radiation dose in trauma
result.setting: Seven Ministry of Health radiology departments (national multicentre)
result.standard: American College of Radiology guidelines for major blunt trauma

cycle1.result: 578 (42.3%) whole-body CTs negative and 789 (57.7%) positive, with 530 (38.8%) major injuries. Mean effective dose 19.98 ± 10.26 mSv for negative scans and 22.41 ± 10.35 mSv for positive scans.

result.other_findings: Road traffic accidents were 66.6% of referrals; fall from height had a higher positive rate. Clinical decision tools, dose monitoring and a national trauma registry were recommended.

result.topic: Enhanced recovery for shoulder arthroplasty length of stay
result.setting: Derby Shoulder Unit, University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: Pre-enhanced recovery: mean LOS 2.38 nights, median 2 nights, single night stay rate 40.2%; complication rate 9.9%.

result.intervention: Enhanced recovery programme via PDSA cycles: MDT-led preoperative class with OT home assessment, new patient information booklet and DVD, standardised anaesthetic/analgesic protocol with carbohydrate and gabapentin loading, and a physiotherapy protocol with sling for comfort only and early safe-zone mobilisation.

cycle2.dates: 6 October 2017 pilot; full roll-out 7 December 2017 to 8 October 2018
cycle2.result: Matched enhanced recovery cohort: mean LOS 1.89 nights (median 2), single night stay rate 49.2%; 15 fewer bed nights; complication rate 7%; OSS and Constant scores similar at 3 and 12 months.

result.other_findings: Adherence to dexamethasone use was only 36% (80% on re-audit of 15 patients) and gabapentin compliance only 24%; 12 patients had discharge delays because social services would not accept pre-admission referral.

result.setting: Trauma unit, Ulster Hospital, Dundonald (district general hospital)
result.standard: Royal College of Surgeons of England handover guidance (2007) plus local orthopaedic-specific criteria

cycle1.result: Poor handover: patient location 57%, responsible consultant 14%, results of significant/pending investigations 29%, co-morbidities 38%, outstanding tasks 38%; one patient not handed over and one nerve injury not handed over.

result.intervention: Trauma-specific paper handover proforma (SHOs informed by email and verbally), then an electronic proforma accessible from any hospital computer, created with IT.

cycle2.result: With the electronic proforma only one criterion fell below 95% (results of pending investigations 82%); no patient safety issues; proforma uptake 100%.

result.other_findings: Intermediate re-audit with the paper proforma (10/02/15 to 16/02/15, 19 patients in text, 17 in abstract): management plan 76%, results of investigations 47%, outstanding tasks 71%, all other criteria at least 80%.

result.setting: Comparison of ten established national hip fracture registries with consensus via the Fragility Fracture Network (FFN) Hip Fracture Audit Special Interest Group
result.country: International (England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scotland; Australia and New Zealand; Republic of Ireland; Germany; the Netherlands; Sweden; Norway; Denmark; Spain)
result.standard: FFN 2014 Minimum Common Dataset (32 fields)

cycle1.result: 215 unique questions across ten registries; only 72 (34%) used in more than one audit and 32 (15%) by more than half. Only 21/32 (65.6%) of 2014 MCD fields used by the majority of audits; only three fields (anaesthetic grade, operation, date/time of surgery) used by all ten; only one registry used all 32 fields.

result.intervention: Revised MCD produced by consensus: 22-field Core 2022 MCD plus 12-field optional Extended 2022 MCD, refined after FFN Asia-Pacific (July 2021) and Global FFN Congress (September 2021) feedback.
result.other_findings: Online feedback: 204/224 respondents (94.1%) agreed with inclusion of the reviewed fields and 157/224 (70.0%) agreed with the core versus extended split.

result.setting: Ten UK NHS trusts, elective primary total hip and knee arthroplasty (prospective multicentre audit)
result.standard: National waste management guidance: infectious (orange) stream only for suspected infectious agents, otherwise offensive (tiger-stripe) and general streams; no numerical target stated

cycle1.result: 92 THAs and 130 TKAs; mean total waste 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste the largest category (9.88 kg THA, 8.68 kg TKA). Only 5/10 trusts used an offensive waste stream and 8/10 used recycling; significant inter-hospital variation in all waste categories (p < 0.001).

result.other_findings: On multivariable regression, hospital site was the main predictor of waste; trusts using offensive waste eliminated nearly all infectious waste. Switching streams estimated to save about £1.38 per THA and £1.22 per TKA.

result.topic: Alcohol withdrawal screening in trauma patients
result.setting: Community level 1 trauma centre (Conemaugh Memorial Medical Center), adult trauma admissions
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 30 (4.5%) had AWS (AWS score ≥ 3). AUDIT-C ≥ 5 predicted AWS with 90.0% sensitivity, 96.2% specificity, PPV 52.9%, NPV 99.5%; AUC 0.989.

result.other_findings: 48 patients (7.3%) were suboptimally managed: 23/51 (45%) with AUDIT-C ≥ 5 were not placed on CIWA-Ar and 25/611 (4.1%) with AUDIT-C < 5 were placed on CIWA-Ar.

result.topic: Online information quality for calcaneal apophysitis
result.setting: Top 50 Google-ranked websites per country on children's heel pain (content analysis)
result.standard: Elements of the DISCERN tool and JAMA instrument; SMOG readability; alignment with systematic review and trial evidence

cycle1.result: 118 (79%) hosted by private health services; mean SMOG 9.3 (SD 4.5); 140 (93%) gave at least one treatment recommendation but only 11 (7%) had all treatment recommendations supported by evidence.

result.other_findings: Only 75 (50%) gave a publication date and 67 (45%) described the condition as benign or self-limiting; some sites advertised surgery, shock wave therapy and laser.

result.setting: Single-site pain management service, Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust (retrospective cohort audit with telephone survey)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 81 (93%) satisfied with SCS; pain improvement group significantly associated with satisfaction (p = 0.010), with all patients in the >50% group satisfied.

result.other_findings: Pain improvement group also associated with sleep (p < 0.001), fatigue (p = 0.001), QoL (p = 0.003) and opioid use (p = 0.010); 49% increased neuropathic pain medication.

result.setting: Morning trauma meeting, Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics, major trauma centre (Salford Royal NHS Foundation Trust)
result.standard: Locally developed 10-domain, 20-point presentation quality score; complete presentation defined a priori as score ≥ 16

cycle1.result: Mean score 11.6 ± 3.0/20; complete presentations 18/75 (24.0%); management plan documented 49/75 (65.3%); tasks allocated 28/75 (37.3%); median clarification prompts 2 (IQR 1-3).

result.intervention: One-page 10-domain structured presentation template expanded from an acronym in the electronic patient record, introduced with a five-minute briefing, laminated copies in the meeting room and inclusion in the junior doctor induction pack.

cycle2.result: Mean score 17.1 ± 2.1/20 (difference 5.5, 95% CI 4.7-6.3; p<0.001); complete presentations 61/75 (81.3%; p<0.001); management plan 72/75 (96.0%); tasks allocated 67/75 (89.3%); median clarification prompts 1 (IQR 0-1).

result.other_findings: Median presentation duration unchanged (2.7 to 2.5 minutes, p=0.18); neurovascular status improved from 34/75 (45.3%) to 66/75 (88.0%). Sustainability beyond the initial period was not assessed.

result.setting: Single emergency department digital X-ray room, busy metropolitan public hospital (Logan Hospital)
result.standard: No established reject rate guideline stated; ALARA principle

cycle1.result: Overall reject rate 10.3% (1,193/11,596) and multiple reject rate 1.3% (147). Highest multiple reject rates among frequent projections: horizontal beam knee 32/380 (8.4%) and horizontal beam hip 17/182 (9.3%).

result.other_findings: Top reasons for rejection were positioning (58.0%) and anatomy cut-off (18.3%); AP pelvis reject rate 22.5% and AP chest 18.1%. Authors recommend staff education and re-audit.

result.topic: Hand and wrist surgical referral compliance with Evidence-based Interventions guidance
result.setting: Single community musculoskeletal service, Greater Manchester
result.standard: 2018 Evidence-based Interventions programme and Greater Manchester local guidance for carpal tunnel release, Dupuytren's release, ganglion excision and trigger finger release; project target ≥85% (provider internal national target 95%)

cycle1.result: Referral compliance 70%, 15% below the provider's internal national average and 25% below its 95% internal target.

result.intervention: Four PDSA cycles over 14 weeks: education session and case discussions, digital folder with clinical referral flowchart, knowledge quiz with case discussions, repeat quiz and Q&A.

cycle2.result: Compliance 71% after PDSA 1, 85% after PDSA 2, 99% after PDSA 3 and 100% in PDSA 4; average compliance improved 16% against the audit, 1% above the 85% target.

result.other_findings: Clinician confidence improved by 15% and quiz scores by 12%; referrals to injection clinics rose 3.2%. Improvement reported as sustained 6 months after the project.

result.topic: INR sample rejection in hip fracture
result.setting: Trauma and Orthopaedics Department, Heartlands Hospital, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust (major trauma centre)
result.standard: Correct filling of 3.2% sodium citrate tubes to maintain 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio, with discard tube first when using butterfly sets; no numerical target stated

cycle1.result: 66/399 INR samples rejected (16.5%, 95% CI 13.2-20.5%); 62 (94%) for underfilling and 4 (6%) for haemolysis.

result.intervention: Education sessions for junior doctors, phlebotomists and nurses on discard-tube use with butterfly sets, routine stocking of short-tubing collection devices, and visual reminder prompts at sampling points.

cycle2.result: 29/261 rejected (11.1%, 95% CI 7.8-15.5%); absolute reduction 5.4 percentage points, relative ~33%, not significant (p ≈ 0.11); 27 (93%) underfilling, 2 (7%) haemolysis.

result.other_findings: Among anticoagulated patients rejection rose from 17.4% to 19.6%; underfilling remained the dominant cause.

result.setting: Kings Mill Hospital, a 650-bed district general hospital (Sherwood Forest Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust); adults presenting to the ED with suspected scaphoid fracture
result.standard: BSSH Scaphoid Standards: review in a specialist fracture clinic within 7 days of presentation, and a dedicated four-view scaphoid radiograph series at initial assessment (target 100% for both)

cycle1.result: Fracture clinic review within 7 days in 68.5% (170/248); four-view scaphoid series in 95.2% (236/248). Scaphoid fracture confirmed in 44 (17.7%); false-negative rate of initial radiographs 22.7% (10/44), false-positive rate 5.2% (13/248).

result.other_findings: Advanced imaging in 29.0% (29 CT, 43 MRI) with median times of 36.5 days (CT) and 30 days (MRI); median time to specialist exclusion of fracture 18.5 days. Clinical examination findings and hand dominance were poorly documented (dominance unrecorded in 66.9%).

result.setting: Nationwide Dutch Hip Fracture Audit (DHFA) registry, more than 95% of Dutch hospitals
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 3.2% (3065) treated nonoperatively. Nonoperative patients were older (median 86 vs 81 years), more often institutionalised (42.4% vs 17.6%) and had more dementia (37.2% vs 15.2%). 7-day mortality 37.6% and 30-day mortality 57.1% in nonoperative patients.

result.other_findings: Registry cohort study, not an audit against a standard. 885 nondisplaced femoral neck fractures were managed nonoperatively despite the Dutch guideline advising operative management, with lower 7-day (23.3%) and 30-day (38.7%) mortality than other fracture types.

result.topic: Implant choice for stable trochanteric hip fractures
result.setting: Six mid-to-large Dutch hospitals in the Dutch Hip Fracture Audit Indicator Taskforce
result.standard: Dutch hip fracture guideline advises extramedullary fixation for stable AO 31-A1 trochanteric fractures

cycle1.result: 138 (16%) treated with extramedullary fixation and 698 (84%) with intramedullary fixation. Mobility with frame/2 supports or better at discharge EMF 77% vs IMF 50%; no significant difference at 3 months (EMF 80% vs IMF 82%).

result.other_findings: Registry outcome comparison rather than an audit. In-hospital complication rates were similar (EMF 40% vs IMF 39%) and 3-month mortality was 16% vs 15%; the authors note low guideline adherence nationally.

result.setting: German Trauma Society (DGU) certified geriatric fracture centres (AltersTraumaZentrum DGU) and the AltersTraumaRegister DGU
result.standard: AltersTraumaZentrum DGU Criteria Catalogue (structures, trauma surgery, geriatric care, interdisciplinary cooperation, quality and risk management)

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Descriptive article on the certification process and registry; nearly 50 centres certified and more than 150 registered. Requirements include geriatric screening on admission or by day 1 after surgery, geriatrician presence at least twice weekly and weekly interdisciplinary meetings.

result.setting: Three public metropolitan hospitals contributing to the Australian and New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry
result.standard: Literature-derived benchmarks for data agreement and completeness (very high if ≥95%, high 90–94%, moderate 80–84%)

cycle1.dates: Records from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2016; abstraction May to August 2017
cycle1.result: Overall data agreement 82.3% (7111/8639 items), moderate; overall data completeness 95.6% (8258/8639), very high. Lowest agreement for ED departure time (27.0%) and time of surgery (33.1%).

result.other_findings: 46.2% of disagreements were information discrepancies, 24.5% missing, 27.3% time/date/number and only 2.0% transcription. Registry completeness was lowest for discharge place of residence (74.2%) and discharge date (77.3%).

result.topic: Enhanced recovery length of stay in hip and knee arthroplasty
result.setting: North Devon District Hospital, elective hip and knee replacement pathway
result.standard: Local SMART aim: 90% of cases mobilising on day 0 and length of stay reduced by 1 day within 1 year, with increased throughput

cycle1.result: Mean length of stay 3.6 days for both total hip and total knee replacement; Model Hospital median length of stay 4.2 days (hips, 41st nationally) and 3.9 days (knees, 34th).

result.intervention: Multidisciplinary Rapid Recovery Group with parallel PDSA cycles: ropivacaine local infiltration protocol, oxycodone MR, preprinted drug charts, Taurus frames and nurse-led mobilisation, stopping routine MSU and TED stockings, and a ring-fenced elective ward.

cycle2.result: Mean length of stay fell to 2.4 days for hips and 2.0 days for knees (p<0.0001); all patients mobilised on day 0 in the most recent 3 months; predicted yearly throughput 560 vs 480.

result.other_findings: Trust moved from 41st to 8th (hips) and 34th to 4th (knees) nationally for length of stay; opioid use per patient fell from about 400 mg to under 300 mg morphine equivalent. Only 3.5% of first mobilisations were by a physiotherapist in the latest 3 months.

result.topic: Image transfer time for neurosurgical referrals
result.setting: Trauma and orthopaedics department, Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust, referring to Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham neurosurgery
result.standard: 100% of NORSe referrals should have images sent to neurosurgery within 1 hour; neurosurgery should review imaging and respond within 6 hours at least 90% of the time

cycle1.result: Mean time from referral to image transfer 18 hours; 36% (n=14) transferred within 1 hour; neurosurgery response averaged 18 hours with 38% (n=14) reviewed within 6 hours.

result.intervention: Image exchange portal software introduced so T&O registrars, then junior doctors, could send images directly without the PACS team; supported by departmental presentation, video demonstration, emailed instructions, QR-code posters and induction teaching.

cycle2.result: Mean time to image transfer 3.6 hours; 61% (n=96) transferred within 1 hour; neurosurgery response averaged 7 hours with 87% (n=138) reviewed within 6 hours; 45% (71) of images sent by the T&O team.

result.other_findings: Intermediate cycle (March to May 2024, n=64): mean transfer 9.3 hours, 28% within 1 hour, 43% reviewed within 6 hours, and only 6.2% of images sent by T&O owing to poor registrar uptake. Neither target was fully met; the abstract quotes 59% within 1 hour.

result.setting: National online clinical-case questionnaire of French physicians, including reference centres for complex bone and joint infection (CRIOACs)
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: CRIOAC response rates 92%, 77% and 53% for the three questionnaires. 32–39% did not give antibiotic prophylaxis despite positive S. aureus documentation; one-stage exchange preferred (72–91%) for late PJI; rifampicin-fluoroquinolone chosen in 70–92% for S. aureus.

result.other_findings: Survey of declared practice rather than an audit against a standard. There was no consensus on total antibiotic duration, with 6 to 12 weeks chosen by most respondents.

result.setting: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, a major trauma centre
result.standard: NICE fractures guidance: manipulation for dorsally displaced distal radius fractures (1.4.5); surgery within 72 hours for intra-articular and within 7 days for extra-articular fractures (1.4.3)

cycle1.result: 90% (27/30) underwent manipulation and plaster in the ED; 3 (10%) went straight to surgery, 2 (6.7%) without a documented reason.

result.intervention: Email to all T&O registrars about NICE guidance, dedicated teaching sessions, and an internal management pathway for distal radius fractures.

cycle2.result: Overall surgical timing compliance 11.6% (5/43): 10% (4/40) of intra-articular fractures within 72 hours (mean 8.6 days) and 33.3% (1/3) of extra-articular fractures within 7 days (mean 6.3 days).

result.other_findings: Cycle 2 measured a different standard (surgical timing) from cycle 1 (manipulation), so the cycles are not directly comparable. Insufficient trauma theatre capacity caused 73.7% (28/38) of delays.

result.topic: Occupational psychological crises among financial auditors
result.setting: Auditors employed in audit firms
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: not reported

result.other_findings: Not a clinical paper: a questionnaire study of accounting auditors reporting that occupational psychological crises were positively associated with organisational future indifference and organisational trauma.

result.setting: University Hospital of North Norway, Tromsø; Level 1 trauma centre, patients with trauma team activation registered in the Norwegian national trauma registry
result.standard: Expert coder group consensus reference standard using the AIS 2005 Update 2008 manual (review of all EHR data and reinterpretation of all imaging); no target stated

cycle1.dates: Patients admitted in 2015; reference standard coding February 2016 to March 2017
cycle1.result: 582 AIS codes in the registry vs 766 in the reference standard. All injuries concordantly coded in 62 (43.1%) patients. 166 missing codes in 71 (49.3%) patients, mostly AIS 1, chiefly EHR information overlooked by coders. 157 discordant codes in 74 (51.4%) patients, mainly head injuries and extremity fractures. Median ISS (9) and NISS (12) identical in registry and reference standard; ISS changed in 52 (36.1%) patients; no significant difference on Bland–Altman regression (ISS p = 0.078, NISS p = 0.656).

result.other_findings: A software error in registry data retrieval omitted 46 duplicate codes and was corrected by the registry; the authors trained trauma physicians in AIS coding and proposed adding coding review to the monthly trauma audit, but no re-measurement is reported.

result.setting: Addenbrooke's Major Trauma Unit, Cambridge University Hospitals; major trauma centre, open talus fractures in skeletally mature patients
result.standard: BOAST 4 guidelines for open fractures (e.g. prophylactic antibiotics within one hour of injury, definitive soft tissue coverage within 72 h, orthoplastic involvement, debridement); no target stated

cycle1.result: 15 open talus fractures in 14 patients. 100% had orthoplastic involvement, initial saline-soaked gauze and occlusive film dressing, functional recovery and rehabilitation advice, and recorded debridement; 60% had debridement using fasciotomy lines. Only 27% received prophylactic antibiotics within one hour of injury and only 27% achieved definitive soft tissue coverage within 72 h (mean 9.7 days in the 7 needing coverage).

result.other_findings: Mainly a cohort comparison: no significant difference between ORIF and tibiocalcaneal fusion in EQ-5D-5L (p = 0.13), FAAM-ADL (p = 0.20), FAAM-Sport (p = 0.34) or infection rate (p = 0.55); deep infection occurred in 7 cases (47%).

result.setting: National Joint Registry (England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Isle of Man, Guernsey); national data quality audit of all NHS and independent sector arthroplasty units
result.standard: Compliance of NJR entries validated against each unit's Patient Administration System; target 95% or higher compliance

cycle1.result: Baseline average organisation-level compliance 92.64% (92.6%), with over 7,000 cases in provider data but missing from the NJR; 9.7% of revision hips missing vs 5.6% of primaries, and 9.8% of revision knees vs 5.1% of primaries.

result.intervention: Annual bidirectional data quality audit cycle: statements of missing cases sent to units for retrospective entry, named data quality lead per unit, data completeness awards and tariff top-up targets, audit reports with action plans to CEOs and clinical leads, unit visits, communications and user guides, and a semi-automated upload platform from 2018.

cycle2.result: Baseline compliance rose year-on-year to 96.0% in 2018/19, reaching 97.9% overall after closure of the audit cycle; 76.4% of units achieved >95% compliance (61.5% of units achieved ≥95% on first run of the 2018/19 audit). 314 units completed the 2018/19 audit.

result.other_findings: Intermediate unit-level baseline compliance was 91.78% (2015/16), 92.46% (2016/17) and 94.12% (2017/18), with missing cases falling from 11,285 to 8,670; a persistent gap remained between primary and revision procedures.

result.topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI
result.setting: Medway Maritime Hospital, Gillingham; district general hospital emergency department without on-site emergency spinal surgery
result.standard: GIRFT National Suspected CES Pathway 2023: emergency MRI within 4 hours of request; local SMART aim of median under 4 hours from ED attendance to MRI within 1 year

cycle1.result: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. At PDSA 1: 38% of MRIs unnecessary, 0.5 CES MRIs/day, time to analgesia 5.3 hours (IQR 3.8–7.0), 9% inappropriately triaged to MEDOCC.

result.intervention: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.

cycle2.dates: PDSA 3, cycles run July 2023 to January 2024
cycle2.result: Approximately 27 patients per cycle. Median ED presentation to MRI 5.7 hours (IQR 4.1–14.3), primary aim not met; GIRFT 4-hour request-to-scan target met in all cycles. Unnecessary MRIs fell from 38% to 18%, CES MRIs 0.5/day to 0.4/day, time to analgesia 5.3 to 4.2 hours (IQR 2.7–7.0), and inappropriate MEDOCC referrals 9% to 0%.

result.other_findings: Time to MRI rose to 9.9 hours in PDSA 2 amid ED pressures and industrial action; 43/81 patients presented at times making same-day MRI unlikely because scanners ran only until 20:00, and by PDSA 3 attendance to MRI request was still a median 3.9 hours.

result.setting: Arthroplasty Clinical Outcomes Registry NSW (ACORN); two major hospitals (A and B) in New South Wales
result.standard: Benchmark of 95.0% for data completeness and accuracy against reabstracted medical record data

cycle1.dates: Surgery in 2012/2013 (first six months of data submission)
cycle1.result: Completeness 99.0% (1259/1272) Hospital A and 99.3% (1589/1600) Hospital B; accuracy 94.0% (2159/2296) Hospital A and 96.1% (2444/2542) Hospital B. 57.1% (28/49) of variables met the 95% accuracy benchmark in A and 74.5% (38/51) in B. Registry captured 93.5% (660/706) of eligible patients.

result.other_findings: Most accuracy discrepancies were in comorbidity (medical history) data, e.g. hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and GIT; only 10.2% (A) and 8.0% (B) of records were entirely error-free. 100 records were sampled; one from Hospital A was excluded.

result.setting: Advanced practice physiotherapist triage services in orthopaedic and rheumatology clinics at 16 major acute hospitals; national database, with re-referral pilot at St Vincent's University Hospital, Dublin
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 13,981 new patients seen by 22 APPs; median wait 167 days (IQR 91–316). APPs made autonomous decisions at 77.2% of appointments; 18.1% required onward referral to orthopaedic or rheumatology consultants; physiotherapy referral 41.5%, investigations 29.3%, injections 4.1%, surgical listing 2.4%. Of 184 patients managed without consultant referral, 12 (6.5%) were re-referred within one year and 20 (10.9%) within two years.

result.other_findings: Knee (23%), lumbar spine (22%) and shoulder (15%) were the commonest presentations; 70% of re-referred patients had no change in management.

result.topic: Fragility fracture recording and bone protection
result.setting: 12 general practices in Crawley, south-east England; primary care, community-based fracture liaison nurse pilot
result.standard: Anticipated pay-for-performance (QOF/Directed Enhanced Service) osteoporosis indicators: register of patients with fragility fracture, and treatment with a bone-sparing agent in those aged 50–74 with confirmed osteoporosis and in those aged 75 and over with a fragility fracture

cycle1.result: Females 50–74 (n=13,519) and ≥75 (n=4,883). Bone-sparing agent in those aged 50–74 with fragility fracture and confirmed osteoporosis 47.9% (23/48); in those ≥75 with fragility fracture 39.5% (118/181). Fragility fracture recorded 8.8% (15/171) aged 50–74 and 0.8% (65/8110) aged ≥75.

result.intervention: Introduction of a community-based fracture liaison nurse who reviewed the practice population meeting the inclusion criteria.

cycle2.result: Bone-sparing agent 84.0% (42/50) aged 50–74 and 70.5% (222/316) aged ≥75 (p<0.001). Fragility fracture recorded 14% (25/178) aged 50–74 (p=0.168) and 2.3% (199/8702) aged ≥75 (p<0.001).

result.other_findings: Recording of smoking and BMI roughly doubled, but DXA scan recording fell (e.g. 2.5% to 1.4% in those ≥75); less deprived patients were more likely to receive DXA scans and more deprived patients bone-sparing agents.

result.setting: Emergency department, City Hospitals Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust; district general hospital, adults 16 and over
result.standard: Royal College of Emergency Medicine guidelines on time to shoulder dislocation reduction (2-hour RCEM clinical standard of 75% for initial attempt at reduction)

cycle1.result: Average triage to confirmed shoulder reduction X-ray 2 hours 25 min (range 1 h 14 min to 5 h 3 min); triage to discharge 3 hours 22 min (range 1 h 46 min to 6 h 39 min); 57% (17/30) sedated for reduction.

result.intervention: Shoulder Reduction Bench (modified Oxford Chair) introduced with three PDSA cycles: training of emergency nurse practitioners, written protocol and flowchart on the intranet, and an online training video.

cycle2.dates: 6 months after project launch (March to September)
cycle2.result: Average triage to confirmed reduction X-ray 1 hour 54 min (31 min, 21% reduction); triage to discharge 2 hours 30 min (52 min, 26% reduction); 18% (7) sedated, a 68% reduction.

result.other_findings: The protocol was not followed in 2 cases (5%, both consultants) and adherence was unclear in 2 more; after restricting use to protocol criteria there were no further complications.

result.topic: Hip fracture follow-up after internal fixation
result.setting: Midland Regional Hospital Tullamore; Irish tertiary referral trauma unit, fracture clinic follow-up after DHS or intramedullary nail
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: 428 outpatient appointments (mean 1.6 per patient); mean 1.13 inpatient and 1.54 outpatient radiographs per patient. 16 (5.8%) had abnormal radiographs and 8 (2.9%) underwent revision surgery; 15/16 (94%) with complications were symptomatic. DNA rate 13.1% costing €1,400; total follow-up cost €92,252 over 3 years.

result.other_findings: Cost analysis rather than audit; the authors propose selective and virtual follow-up and note that Irish integrated care pathway guidance advises routine follow-up 6 weeks after DHS or IM nail fixation.

result.setting: Galway University Hospital fracture clinics; tertiary care hospital, consultant-led
result.standard: BOAST Guideline 7 (fracture clinic services), assessed with a patient questionnaire adapted from the RCSI SWOPS questionnaire; no target stated

cycle1.result: Average wait for appointment 3.55 days (85 hours); wait to see doctor in clinic 56.81 minutes; doctors rated excellent 75%; X-ray facilities inadequate 34.7%; waiting area inadequate 44.93%; overall experience excellent 50.72%.

result.intervention: Changed fracture clinic appointment rotation, increased doctors on site, ensured patients returning from X-ray saw the same doctor, optimised follow-up X-ray process and increased waiting area seating from about 40 to 50; findings on X-ray location passed to management.

cycle2.result: Average wait for appointment 3.21 days (77.04 hours); wait to see doctor 52.55 minutes; doctors rated excellent 73.9%; X-ray facilities inadequate 32.79%; waiting area inadequate 41.49%; overall experience excellent 53.55%.

result.other_findings: The X-ray department remained a five-minute, partly outdoor walk from the clinic and waiting area ratings stayed poor; the year of data collection is not stated.

result.setting: Six accident and emergency departments; regional study led by the Northern Ireland Plastic and Maxillofacial Unit, Ulster Hospital
result.standard: not reported

cycle1.result: Isolated hand or wrist injuries made up 6.6% of attendances; male:female ratio 2.2:1; mean age 26.4 years (men) and 29.2 years (women); 16.3% caused by falls, 15% by sport and 7% work/machinery related; 13.3% referred to specialities for further treatment.

result.other_findings: Abstract only; right and left hands were injured almost equally, with the dominant hand more often injured.

result.topic: Distal radius fracture time to fixation
result.setting: Lincoln County Hospital, United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust; retrospective service evaluation of adult distal radius ORIF
result.standard: BOAST distal radius fracture standards: unstable intra-articular fractures fixed within 72 hours of injury; extra-articular fractures within seven days; re-displaced fractures within 72 hours of decision to operate

cycle1.result: Overall BOAST timing compliance 12% (3/25); extra-articular 100% (2/2), intra-articular 4.3% (1/23). Virtual fracture clinic pathway 0% (0/17) vs traditional trauma meeting 37.5% (3/8) (Fisher's exact p = 0.0243; OR 0.045, 95% CI 0.002-0.93).

result.other_findings: 94% (16/17) of virtual fracture clinic patients had a face-to-face clinic review before listing vs 0% (0/8) via the trauma meeting. Authors propose a direct-listing escalation protocol from virtual fracture clinic and a re-audit with timestamps at each pathway step.

result.setting: Major Trauma Centre for the South East of England, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, Brighton; orthoplastic service
result.standard: BOAST 4 open lower limb fracture standards, e.g. IV antibiotics within 1 h of injury; debridement within 12 h for high-energy and 24 h for other fractures; definitive soft tissue cover within 72 h; gentamicin on induction; photographs; saline lavage

cycle1.result: Debridement within 24 h 81% (108/133); high-energy within 12 h 25% (15/60); mean time to first debridement 18.77 h. Definitive fixation/closure within 72 h 75% (95).
